title: The Warrior in All of Us
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster takes up Kakusan Shidō, the thirteenth-century founder of Tokeiji Convent, whose story from The Hidden Lamp has her drawing a ten-inch dagger before her teacher during the transmission ceremony. IkuShun reads Laura del Valle's commentary on that story, including del Valle's boot-camp Rinzai training in Mexico City and the day she drove a mother to bring her children back from the father. From there, IkuShun recalls speaking up for patients as a diabetes educator and asks where courage comes from, returning to del Valle's line about cutting off the fear of self-concern. IkuShun closes with a conversation with a teacher about Rosa Parks, whose clarity may have left no room for choice.

sentences.text: An unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million to see and listen to, to remember and accept, to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.
Thank you for coming, everybody, and people on Zoom.
Hi, Scott.
Hi, Mary.
Thank you.
Tonight, I'm going to continue talking about our women ancestors.
If this is your first time here, we're in a little series talking about our ancestors, but primarily focusing on women ancestors.
I know Chris did a couple of talks on women ancestors, so I'm going to continue that historic part of the talk.
But then I want to look at the contemporary teachers and somebody who commented on this particular person in the Hidden Lamp.
Does everyone know about the Hidden Lamp?
It's a really wonderful collection of stories, one hundred thirty-five or something, of women ancestors, but each one has a commentary from a contemporary teacher.
I'm going to be looking at her commentary as well.
I named the talk Kakuzan Shiro, who is the person I'm going to talk about, and the warrior energy in all of us, because I want to continue exploring this warrior energy a little bit.
Continuing with the ancestors first, this person's name was Kakuzan Shiro, and she was alive from 1252 to 1305.
I want to continue looking at some contemporary teachers, particularly Laura DeValle, who commented on this little blurb about Kakuzan, so we'll talk about her in a little bit, too.
Then I just really want to look at our warrior energy that's in all of us: how does it arise?
Where does it come from?
What factors came together to bring about this manifestation?
We'll look at that.
So bear with me with the historic piece first.
Let's find out a little bit more about Kakuzan.
Kakuzan Shiro was a part of the warrior class of women, referred to as *onna-musha*, referring to female ancestors in pre-modern Japan.
I don't know if you have seen any pictures of these Japanese women warriors, but they're fierce.
It's really interesting this period of time in Japan where there was a lot of war, a lot of violence, and people were trained to protect their own, their family, their children, their home.
It was a very interesting time.
Against the typical outlook of the weak female, these women were warriors, and they were trained to use weapons to protect their household.
As such, they always carried this ten-inch dagger in their kimono or whatever it was that they wore.
Kakuzan also became a nun later on, and she trained at the notoriously tough Rinzai monastery in Kakuji.
Here are a few words from the write-up in Hidden Lamp: *In the transmission ceremony, Kakuzan Shiro took the seat in front of the altar, and the monks asked her questions to test her skill.
When it was the head monk's turn, her teacher, he was her teacher, Tokei, given the name Peach Tree Valley, challenged her.
In our lineage, anyone who receives Inka must give a discourse in the sutras.
Are you really capable of doing that?

Shiro then pulled out her ten-inch dagger, carried by all women of the warrior class and held it in front of his face, and said, In the lineage of our master should teach the sutras, but I am a woman of the warrior line, and I speak the Dharma face to face with my dagger drawn.
What need do I have of books?
He persisted with another question.
What was your original understanding before your parents were born, which is a very famous koan.
She answered by sitting in silence with her eyes closed.*
Then she said, "Do you understand?"
The head monk answered with a verse: *Here in Peach Tree Valley, a wine gourd has been drained to the last drop.
Drunken eyes see ten miles of flowers.
Don't ask me to explain.* Shiro replied, "Was I not directed to the way even before the births of my mother and father?"
So she got Inka transmission.
Shiro was also known for creating this first temple that granted divorces to women from their husbands.
Despite the prevailing attitudes that claimed that women were weak and whimsical and only fit to be submissive to men, many women became very powerful in this pre-Tokugawa era.

That little blurb was from a book called *Zen Women Beyond Tea Ladies, Iron Maidens, and Macho Masters* by Grace Sheerson, who is also someone well known to us and a really wonderful teacher, so I might talk about her next month a little.
Prior to and during her lifetime, samurai class women were known for their physical and spiritual strength in surviving war and chaos.

As Grace Sheerson says in her book, *Zen Women*, Kakuzan would have been affected by stories recounting the powerful stance of these women who protected themselves and their children, at times fought alongside their husbands, and sometimes turned to the ordination to survive and heal from the wounds of war.
Kakuzan Shiro founded Tokeiji Convent, and it's in Kamakura.
After the death of her husband, the shogun Tokimune, and her son inherited the father's position and sponsored the building of this temple.
But shortly after Kakuzan was installed as abbess, her son ordered the killing of many of her birth family because he had fear that they would not be loyal.
Kakuzan then established, I think partly out of that suffering, Tokeiji as a refuge for women seeking asylum.
Later the temple took on women who needed to initiate divorce and had no legal means.
During her time as reigning abbess, Kakuzan developed a practice called Mirror Zen to address women's interest in their physical appearance.

As we learn from nuns of the Buddha as well as the popularity of contemporary cosmetic opportunities, this is also Grace Sheerson's words: *Women are often taught that their physical beauty is their most prized possession and that maintaining their appearance is their primary concern.
Furthermore, by using seductive abilities, women can exercise power by seducing or influencing powerful men.

And early Buddhist monks were taught to work on their sexual desire and their resistance to the reality of impermanence by meditating on the woman's decomposing body before their eyes.* A corresponding practice developed by the women at Tokeiji was Mirror Zen, the encouragement to see through their feelings and attachments to physical form by meditating in front of a mirror.
Instructions were to look deeply into one's nature and ask, "Where is a single feeling, a single thought in the mirror image in which I gaze?"

I feel as though Kakuzan used her courage to set up this temple where women could not only take refuge from abusive marriages, a really radical action at the time, but also to develop a way to see more deeply into who and what they really were, encouraging an understanding into the nature of being, including the unconditioned world of reality.
That's a little bit about Kakuzan.

In just an FYI, the temple continued with its ability to grant divorces for about six hundred years, which is pretty amazing, until 1873 when a new law was approved and the Court of Justice started to handle the cases.
I wonder how that went after that.
Anyway, the temple also remained a nunnery for over six hundred years and men could not enter until 1902 when a man became avid.
Tokeiji came under the supervision of Enkakuji, which was the first temple that she joined, I think.
I want to shift now and take a look at Laura DeValle's response to Kakuzan.
I'll read some of the comments in this selection, in her selection.
Laura DeValle, many of you may know, is the founder of Mardejade in Mexico, where Norman Fischer goes.
He's gone for about twenty-five or thirty years in December, and it's to that place.
It's because of this woman who founded Mardejade that they go there.
As I read her comments and story, I thought about the manifestation of courage in this contemporary Laura as well.
The very first couple of lines that Laura comments on, she says, "Kakuzan lived in a world of violence filled with uncertainty.
She learned to cut off the fear of self-concern to defend others."
I want to come back to that statement in a little while.
As I read on, I found that Laura also went through a formal warrior training in the 1960s with the first Japanese Rinzai Zen teacher to come to Mexico City.
Takata's eyes twinkled with humor, but his zendo was run like a boot camp.

I learned to face my own terrors over and over as the Jikijitsu, guardian of the temple, usually a Mexican man acting like a samurai, stalked the zendo like a tiger, ready to pounce on whoever dared to shift even slightly.
I don't know if anybody's been to a Rinzai temple, but I remember this friend of mine who used to sit with me a while ago.
She started sitting at a Rinzai temple, and anytime she would even move her finger a little, he'd say, "Maintain Mudra!
Maintain Mudra," very strict.
It was like that.

The sharpness of this strict practice cut through everything I was protecting about myself, Laura said, and pushed me to my limits, to the point I thought I would explode until I found a limitlessness and became sure of myself.
My own dagger was drawn.
She says that Maestro Takata didn't teach much doctrine or establish elaborate rituals.
In essence, he gave us one koan: "How can we help with the poverty and suffering around us?"
This question would shape my life.
Like Kakuzan, I was born into a line of women warriors.
My grandmother and mother were immigrants to the U.S., who as single mothers became fearless for the sake of their children.
Although I was raised in Mexico City and Chicago, I ended up working as a doctor in rural Mexico, where many single mothers struggle for the sake of their children.
Laura recalls a story.
Isabel came to my clinic for help.
She was a thin woman in her late twenties with her hand over her mouth as she spoke to cover her few decaying teeth.
She said that her spouse had taken her children to live with him and his prostitute girlfriend.
My mind was racing.
You're a doctor, not a cop, you have no magic powers, you're not a tough guy with a gun, so what do you think you can do?
Isabel looked down at the ground despondently.
I said, "Get in the car and let's go get him."
The spouse wasn't home and the girlfriend turned over the kids without resistance.
An hour later, the spouse was at the clinic looking for me.
Isabel and the kids hid.
I came out of the clinic to meet him.
"Once the knife is drawn, there is no turning back.
The knife demands that you pay attention to whatever unfolds."
We stared at each other for a long time, breathing heavily.
Before he spoke, "I should kill you, but you're a decent woman, you fed my kids, and I don't kill decent people," and he left.
Shortly after, he did kill someone and was sent to jail.

But she says, working as a doctor for more than thirty years in a country with extreme poverty, lack of social services, and blatant government corruption, I have been called into action by my neighbors countless times.
I've responded to medical emergencies, domestic violence, human rights abusers, and organized town protests at public meetings.
I lack the specialized knowledge to deal with most of the situations that confront me.
But experts are scarce in this neck of the woods.
I could have become paralyzed or expounded Buddhist doctrine and done nothing, or turned away, assuring myself that someone else could deal with it, excuse me, better than I.
Instead, I simply do my best that I can on the spot.
This is my way of living with the dagger drawn.
After reading that, I was curious about the components of courage and what is needed to act.
We all have that warrior energy within us.
How does it arise in some situations and not others?
Just a day ago, as I was writing up this talk, I heard somebody on YouTube vlogging, and she was saying, "Everyone keeps telling me, 'Oh, you're so brave.
Oh, you're so courageous,' but whatever she did, she said, 'I simply had no choice.'" I've been thinking about that.
Do we act in this courageous way when we have no choice?
I think that we do.
Let me explain.
Often, I think there are things in life that are exactly that.
Maybe some of you old timers remember a song by Pete Seeger long ago called, "Oh, had I a golden thread and a needle so fine, I'd weave the bravery of women giving birth."
The story continued, and I thought, yeah, that's certainly a situation where you can't do anything about it.
I mean, you have no choice.
You have to be courageous as you're giving birth.
So I think a lot of situations are like that.
I want to think about some more.
I think about some of the things I've done, and some were externally demanded of me, like being a mandated reporter and having to call social services when I saw abuse or neglect.
In many ways, this external mandate made it easier to act.
Yes, I just simply had to.
But my greatest courage in my career, I think, came from stepping up into situations where I could have been quiet.
These came from being a specialist in insulin management, in particular, as a diabetes educator.
I was an expert developed from years of experience.
Even though all the recommendations ultimately had to come through the physicians' sign-off, most often with the physicians and caregivers that I worked with, they came from my recommendations.
Truthfully, not many medical professionals really have this depth of understanding in this area because people have to, in general, PCPs have to focus on a lot of different general things.
It takes a really focused understanding to work with some insulin management, especially for type one diabetics.

It was in this area that I had the specialty and in order to make the best adjustments for those using insulin, I was the patient's advocate and routinely the physicians trusted me, had no qualms about taking my recommendations.

However, I encountered not so infrequently the need to step up and be willing to speak and convince the physicians for the patient about certain regimens and why they needed that and why they would work, and they could have really significant effects on their life.
If there were mistakes that were made, or they could be potentially very serious.
I want to go back to the line from Laura DeValle's comment on Kakuzan: "She learned to cut off the fear of self-concern."
As I look back on some of these experiences and look at what causes and conditions were present for my actions to manifest, I see a couple significant ones and truly a feeling that I had no choice.

Of course, the underlying preparedness for these actions came from background knowledge and experience, but the great impetus for the action was the above statement to cut off the fear of self-concern to defend others.
At the time of the action, I was very much aware of the importance of self-concern.
At the time of the action, there was no room in my mind for other thoughts.
For a moment, perhaps, I did allow thoughts to enter, the rationalizing or perhaps doubts in the same way that they entered for a moment into Laura's mind.
But in the same way as Laura, I realized that there was no maybe someone else could do it, or maybe they're going to be okay anyway.
I knew that no one else could do it and that unless I made a stance, the person would very likely not be okay.
I had a sense of clarity in those particular situations.
When it is even more urgent, like say somebody jumps into the water to save another being, there is nothing in their mind.
Perhaps there's not a thought at all, just a clarity, a knowing that fills their mind and heart.
And so I think that perhaps another component, though, is clarity.
At those times of action in myself, it was very clear to me that this is what I had to do.
I think if we're unsure about something, if we give even the littlest bit of room for doubt, I think that's what I had to do.
I think if we're unsure about something, if we give even the littlest bit of room for doubt, we may not be able to act.
And that happens to me all the time, as soon as I think, "Oh, maybe," then there's that, it's no longer not a choice.
I was really thinking about that.

I was talking to my teacher, Ryushin and Andrea, about this too the other day, and she offered the thought that, for instance, Rosa Parks, for example, if she did not have the clarity about what was right, she would not have had the clarity or the courage to act.
I think it was very clear in her mind.
So I ask you, what do you think?
When we act with courage, do we even have a choice?
Where does this energy come from?
What needs to be in place for it to manifest?
